It took me almost 10 years to conclude the trilogy, and I'm glad I did. It's clear this is a final entry, with many things ending including the mighty Redbeard. Maybe things are a bit hazy, but I think more than ever you have to face choices where you don't have good outcomes. Will you become a puppet to various sides, a bloodthirsty monster, a hypocrite who smiles at everyone, or maybe dare talk back and face the wrath of the most powerful Keeper on the lands.

A story ends with this chapter, although there are still all the remaining stories of Spiderweb Software waiting. It's funny how when I first started it, the Avadon games were the new fancy ones, and now that I finish it, they have become the oldest of the modern Spiderweb games.

At last, a fitting conclusion to this magnificent saga! Jeff has once again demonstrated his boundless creativity and prolific talent as a writer. The plot is masterfully crafted, with quests and decisions that are as captivating as they are thrilling. The choices you make seem to carry weight, influencing the game in intriguing ways - though I’ve only scratched the surface with a single playthrough.

The Avadon series shines with its variety of classes, each offering unique builds enhanced by an array of interesting and genuinely useful items and artifacts. The ability to assemble a team of three from a diverse roster of companions adds another layer of depth and flexibility. It's refreshing not to be locked into a fixed party, as you can tailor your team to suit each mission.

However, it’s clear the game was developed on a modest budget. The graphics remain largely unchanged from earlier installments, and while it performs better than Avadon 1 and on par with Avadon 2, there’s no new music, voice acting, or visual updates. The reuse of icons, sprites, and assets might not bother some - myself included - but in 2025, I can understand how it could be a drawback for others.

As the game progresses, some battles can become increasingly frustrating due to the overwhelming number of enemies, each unleashing area-of-effect attacks and spells. However, the Tinkermage is so incredibly overpowered that I genuinely believe it’s possible to finish the game without relying on companions - talk about a one-person army, haha!

I highly recommend these games, but it's best to take breaks between each one. Their similarities can feel repetitive if played back-to-back.

"Avadon 3: The Warborn" concludes the trilogy, offering a worthy continuation of the previous installments. In the canonical ending of the second part, Redbeard remains the Keeper of Avadon but is later removed by the Alliance Council. The events of the third part take place several years later, as the war between the Alliance and the Farlands reaches a stalemate.

Redbeard's return to the periphery becomes a catalyst for changes in the war. The main character, a Hand, finds themselves at the center of events when Redbeard starts to act. According to the ancient laws of the Alliance, only the slayer of the previous Keeper can become the new Keeper. However, the Council appointed Protus as the acting Keeper, deeming Redbeard incompetent and blaming him for starting the war.

The player must choose between two strong leaders. On one hand, Redbeard, who has a clear plan and achieves real results but whose methods are brutal and who is willing to sacrifice his people. On the other hand, Protus is a reasonable, diplomatic, and just leader, supported by the Alliance Council and providing unprecedented funding for Avadon.

The main intrigue of the game lies in maneuvering between these two characters. The player's decisions can lead to the victory or downfall of the Alliance. Throughout the storyline, the player must sequentially eliminate threats from various enemies of the Alliance, including the Khemerians, the Wildrim rebels, the Warborn alliance (hill-folk, ogres, titans), and the main antagonist from the Tawon Empire.

The plot also develops through the opinions of the main character's companions, which can lead to conflicts, but experienced players manage to manipulate them until the very end.

Traditionally for the series, at the end of the game, you can fight Redbeard for the title of Keeper. In "Avadon 3," this battle can be easier if actions are taken throughout the game to weaken him.

The main disappointment of the game is the lack of significant innovations in gameplay mechanics. The only new feature is abilities that temporarily apply effects to surfaces, affecting anyone who walks over them.

"Avadon 3: The Warborn" concludes the trilogy with an engaging storyline and deep moral dilemmas, despite the lack of new gameplay mechanics.

The Avadon series has replaced Baldur's Gate/Neverwinter Nights as my favourite crpg franchise. The storytelling is rich and deep, the character progression is satisfying, and the combat is fun and surprisingly tactical. The exploration is pseudo-realtime (there seems to be a system of "rounds" or "ticks" under the hood, but it's effectively real time).. but when combat happens, it becomes turn based.

My favourite aspect of the game is precisely its *lack* of a "hold shift to highlight interactable objects" type thing. I've always hated those in RPGs as I feel they cheapen the exploration experience and can turn the game into a mindless click fest. Glad to see that missing from this franchise.

If you like story-rich, narrative-driven rpgs with TONS of content (took me 47 hours to complete, and apparently I barely scratched the surface with the sidequests) and some fun tactical combat, I'd highly recommend the Avadon series - to which Avadon 3: The Warborn is a satisfying conclusion. 

Part of me was a bit sad to see the game finally end, but the developer has a large catalogue of similar-looking games, so I'm excited to try those.

J'ai décidé de mettre une recommandation à ce jeu, mais attention, il n'est pas forcément à mettre entre toutes les mains.

Déjà, il s'agit d'une création de Spiderweb, l'entreprise de Jeff Vogel. Si vous ne connaissez pas le bonhomme, une vidéo de la GDC lui est dédiée et est très informative. Un dossier lui a aussi été consacré dans un Canard PC. 
Si on doit résumer : on a ici affaire à l'exemple presque ultime de l'artisan du CRPG qui travaille le genre en indé depuis de nombreuses années et s'est formé un groupe de suiveurs qui aiment son univers, ses méthodes de création (la récupération est très importante ici, on peut dire que ces jeux sont écolos) et ses tics.

Avadon était donc il y a quelques années une nouvelle série de jeux de Spiderweb, le début d'une trilogie qui se termine ici. Toute l'intrigue tourne autour d'Avadon, forteresse qui est le siège de la police d'un pacte entre plusieurs puissances frontalières. Comme dans les épisodes précédents, on y incarne une Main, un personnage entre l'émissaire et le soldat, envoyé en première ligne pour résoudre les problèmes, soit par le dialogue, soit par la manière forte, soit par un subtil mélange des deux.

Pour ne pas perdre les nouveaux venus, rien de ce qui a pu être fait dans les deux précédents jeux n'a d'impact sur cet épisode, comme c'était déjà le cas dans le précédent opus. Bon, la question ici n'est peut-être pas celle de l'accessibilité, car on ne parle pas de jeu très beginner-friendly à la base, mais nous avons peut-être plutôt affaire à un problème de complexité vu la variété des choix possibles dans les précédents jeux.

Et en fait, il est comment ce jeu ? Et bien c'est un CRPG très old-school qui fera mal à certains yeux (certains assets sont réutilisés depuis le premier Avadon, voire peut-être depuis encore avant) avec un système simple (4 caractéristiques, des compétences qui s'améliorent avec des points glanés lors de la montée de niveau, etc...) mais qui permet des combats tactiques souvent velus.

Car voilà en quelque sorte le coeur de la création Vogelienne : ces jeux sont pensés pour offrir un vrai challenge tactique et des affrontements parfois longs face à des boss tortueux. Sur les forums officiels, les échanges sur les habitudes de Vogel et ses éléments cachés à tout bout de champ sont légions. C'est très sympathique comme ambiance, mais je peux aussi comprendre que certains puissent trouver ça rébarbatif.

Des combats à la difficulté parfois extrêmement importantes, des énigmes souvent tordues et un système de jeu un peu archaïque, il faut aimer. Moi c'est mon cas. Mais faites attention si vous voulez vous y risquer. Il est très facile de jeter l'éponge. Rassurez-vous, si vous le faites, je ne serais pas le premier à vous jeter la pierre.

Ahh Avadon. Though I'm near the end game, I have to give this one a thumbs down. Spiderweb games are charming but walk a fine line between being too easy or incredible frustration. While this game is to tie up lose ends from the rest of the trilogy, it feels too much of a retread. The four fronts is an interesting idea, but the game never gives a sense of urgency the way Avernum 2 did where you were the underdog against an overwhelming force. Khalida and Natalie return as party companions but I really found Khalida's arc baffling compared to her in Avadon 2.

Admittedly I played a shaman this time which is still an underpowered class. Late game and admittedly some optional bosses felt too gimmicky with plenty of foes immobilizing you, summons tons of goons and the over abundance of environmental effects that damage you over time. In and of themselves they can be fine in an rpg but here are limited ways to mitigate them in this game, so all combined combat can feel annoying. Plus many foes feel like HP bloating where the result of the fight is a forgone conclusion but they take forever to die. It ends up feeling not exciting or challenging but more of a tedious chore.

Jeff Vogel fixed the leveling system and made it more streamlined (thank you!), yet in the end I couldn't be bothered to finish this. The ratio of annoyance to fun (which all games have none are perfect) was too high for me to want to continue.

Runs mostly smooth on linux.  There was slowdown during large fights, but nothing like it was in Avadon 2 (1 was still the smoothest).  There did seem to be some missing audio (music was there, but I think there's supposed to be background noises in towns such as people talking).  Nothing that really ruined my experience.

Avadon 3 sees some changes from Avadon 1 & 2.  No longer do you reach max level (30) long before the end (provided you do all content). In fact, I think only 1 or 2 characters reached it before the final fight and 2 more during the final fight with the rest at level 29.   The skill trees have been reworked with new skills and while there are still 3 trees for each class, no longer do you need to get two prerequisites to get the first tier in each tree. Instead, you just need the first skill in the tree.

I found that unlike Avadon 2, the combat was far better balanced. No longer are there fights with large number of enemies who can cast charm spells at you like I remember from the end of Avadon 2.  Also, it felt like enemies took forever to kill without actually being a threat (beyond the Charm spells).  Instead, I actually felt like the fights in 3 were fair.  They actually felt like a challenge without feeling cheap.  One example is that new skills include areas of the ground that would be impacted by something (i.e. acid pools where you get acid damage, ice pools that give ice damage, etc.).  There are a few boss fights that worked like puzzles because you had a boss, minions, and the area you fight in would have some sort of hazard in the ground.  Sometimes it was a race to kill as fast as possible, sometimes you could play defensively and just outlast the enemy.

The story was also quite a satisfying ending to the Trilogy - finally you clear up all loose ends from the prior games and finally you can fight Redbeard and it actually means something (kill him in Avadon 1 & 2 and he is still in 3 anyway).  The only thing is that I'm not sure I would recommend playing 1 & 2 even though it's a Trilogy. I just found 3 to be that much enjoyable and I felt like you don't miss much by skipping them.

Ok, before I start - lets get this out of the way.  You really should only play this game if you played the first two otherwise you may find yourself lost or not nearly invested at whats at stake here.  The story writing is great, but without playing the first two the impact of everything happening in the final chapter may not seem as big of deal.

I say that because you won't get the full figure of RedBeard's Madness, or how unlikeable Protus actually is for a guy who initially seems likeable, the perspectives of two of your Companions Nathalie and Khalida who are from the first two games, and the overall love hate relationship you find yourself with Avadon and being a corrupt Federal Police Force in a Fantasy Setting.

You face Moral Decisions of course, like the other two and they are just as gray and complicated as before, though this time around you seem to be able to pull more weight in hopefully trying to influence Avadon for the better... or worse.  But more importantly you get to see the ultimate closing chapter and fate of Avadon.

The gameplay has been streamlined and the leveling up has being simplified a little bit, less decisions but less opportunities to screw over your build.  It's pretty straightforward now and hammered out some of the loose ends and more useless options.

The graphics are mostly the same, minor tweaks... though still the Spiderweb Signature setup.  The writing and mechanics carry the game.  Though the background sounds is still as immersive as ever.  There are lots of references to the first two games, it's nice to see familiar faces...and kill some of them.

Overall, get it but only after you finished the first two and ready to see where it all ends.

Everyone agrees this king of low budget games don't really rely on pretty graphics, but rather on an enjoyable gameplay or - in the case of Spiderweb Software games - on a strong writing and roleplay experience. However, after finishing the two previous episodes of this serie, I find Avadon 3 kind of desappointing. Sure, the game provides so many hours of gameplay and - somewhat - fun, but the story, the plot, the character development and choices/consequences, which I think are the most important elements of RPGs, are rather weak. There are a lot of text, which is good, but the amount of actual informations that would help to build those elements above cited are insignificant. For example, instead of introducing new and interesting characters, the writer keeps bringing back those old nemesises that were not even that interesting to begin with. Similarly, rather than having a dialogue that flesh out the story/plot, you only have those obvious and irrelevant questions such as "what are you doing today?" or "how did you get that scar?" and the worse is that the answers are mostly irrelevant to the story. And when it seems that the player is given an important choice like chosing or not this-important-character side, if you make the "wrong" choice, the choice that doesn't match the writer's agenda, it's simply Game Over, the game ends! In other words, there is no choice, there is only one path...

Anyway, long story short, I came for the story and the roleplay experience, but I stayed for the dopamine kick provided by the loot, the level up system and the boss fights. Now I get why most people prefer Avernum over Avadon, at least the former is straightfoward: no roleplay ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, just adventure.

[h1]GNU/Linux[/h1]
При большом количестве участников боя движок подтормаживает, но в целом игра в оконном режиме работает без нареканий. La gestione dell'inventario rimane però sempre deficitaria (si fa tutto a mano e dopo avere raccolto tantissimi oggetti è un casino).

La storia riprende da dove era rimasta in sospeso nel secondo, quindi è consigliabile giocarli di fila dal primo al terzo, arrivando finalmente ad una conclusione.

La mia sensazione rimane la solita: sebbene il giocatore abbia una certa libertà nel decidere gli eventi nella parte finale del gioco (e degli altri due) sembra quasi che lo sviluppatore VOGLIA che la storia sia quella che interessa a lui. Forse mi aspettavo una conclusione più soddisfacente piuttosto che il racconto di una guerra che alla fin fine lascia un poco l'amaro in bocca. La scrittura rimane comunque eccellente e l'autore tiene alti i toni fino alla fine, non lasciando mai nulla sulla sufficienza (come invece fanno altri man mano che un gioco va verso il finale).

Many, many years and probably about 20 games later, Vogel releases his finest game to date. A lot of people who look at Spiderweb's titles as being the same over and over again most likely haven't played enough of them to see the subtle differences. There are a couple things that set Avadon 3: The Warborn apart from previous titles. One, it's slightly more accessible than previous entries. The character leveling and skill trees aren't quite as involved. This may offend some of the most hardcore RPG fanatics, but may help newer players get into the characters a bit more without feeling overwhelmed. Also, while still being a fairly open game, progression feels a bit more pointed, and less "all over the place" like the earlier Avernum games. I can appreciate both of Vogel's styles completely, the mass chaos of the Avernum sytling and the simplified, slightly more streamlined Avadon entries. Without ruining the story, I'd say by the end I'm completely satisfied with the way Vogel ended the Avadon series. Lots of twists and turns, and plenty of choice and consequence, and certainly multiple endings, depending on how you handle certain events. The game took a bit less time to complete than Avadon 2: The Corruption, and that's okay. Finishing it never felt like a chore, and makes me look forward to playing whatever he comes up with next. Highly recommended to older gamers and younger players who prefer substance over flash.

[b] Avadon 3: The Warborn [/b] is an old-school turn-based rpg with exploration and combat as it’s primary focus, well balanced by character interactions, vivid and constant world-building through descriptions and textlogs, and the occasional equipment upgrading. The option in classes and a wide array of abilities helps keep the encounters engaging and allows light tactical planning on medium-to-large scale battles (especially on higher difficulty levels).
 Following the well-established molds of the Geneforge and Avadon sagas, Avadon offers a huge world and interesting characters to populate it. This game’s particularity comes in the form of a more focused storytelling that takes precedence over the free-form exploration. The story itself revolves around the player as a lowly Pact soldier that gets elevated to the status of Hand of Avadon, being given the power and the responsibility to end the war with the Farlands. How this is brought about is up to you: crush your enemies mercilessly, or subdue them by aiding in your common struggles. The sum of your positioning towards your superiors and companions determines  later-game outcomes.

Between all the aspects that come out upon hours of gameplay, some excel.
[u] Things A3 got right [/u]:
[list]
[*]The “low budget GoT” feel of the story, having a gray-scaled political struggle at the center of your narrative, is well-paced and gripping;
[*]The retooled Vitality system and Talent upgrade paths shake up the fighting and leveling in relation to the previous iterations;
[*]The returning companions and npc’s from A1&2, as well as the cleverly written (if a bit on the short side) party interaction.
[/list]

[u] Things A3 didn’t get right[/u]:
[list]
[*]The world could be more flushed out. The lack of bartering, interaction with less important npcs and a comprehensive font of knowledge (outside the painfully short codex descriptions) about the culture and political behavior of each country and people leaves too much to the imagination;
[*]Few minor dialogue inconsistencies (companions referring to early quests half-way through the game);
[*]The extended encounters (enemies with too much health and not enough damage output can easily become a slog rather than a challenge);
[*]The lack of a soundtrack, slightly offset by the mild ambient sounds.
[/list]

Avadon 3 is a great game. The fact that story events are the direct outcome of the previous games’ plots should be enough incentive to get through the previous games first, even though it’s not strictly necessary. All around, the positives of the game far outweigh the weak spot that are almost inherent to this type of indie, like graphics and sound (On regards to which, by the way, you can always improve your experience by having your favorite dungeon synth/dark ambient playlist at hand, it makes the wandering around far more enjoyable).

It's likely that anyone reading reviews for Avadon 3 has likely played the first two, and perhaps some other games by Spiderware Software too. "More of the same" is an accurate description, since there haven't been any huge changes to the game, and it's a continuation of the story that began and progressed in the first and second games. This time round, Avadon finds itself in the awkward situation of having two keepers, as well as fighting a prolonged, fractured war on several different fronts from enemies both within and without the Pact. You're a young Hand who's been dropped into the middle of this confusing situation and - as with any other Spiderweb game - you're supposed to navigate through the events of the game via combat and intrigue while deciding which of several imperfect factions deserves your support the most.

The UI is mostly the same, with a few cosmetic changes here and there (nothing that'll confuse anyone who's played the first two games). The mechanics feel very similar too. The only major changed I noticed was that you now recover all mana after a fight, instead of some of it (in my opinion it makes the game easier, seeing as now no longer have to "hold back" your most powerful spells, since all your spell energy will recover after a fight anyway, except for a tiny slither in the event that you get knocked unconscious). The skill trees have been changed slightly, but it's nothing too major. There's some new spells for mages, although I feel like one AoE one in particular is a little OP.

Although I get the impression I'm only about a quarter of the way into the game, I can already feel my loyalties being tugged in at least three different directions. In between trying to end both a civil and a foreign war, there are plenty of opportunities to make money, piss people off and gather potted plants for your lovelorn enemies. There are several new companions to get to know, along with some returning faces, and following in the style of the previous games, they all seem to have their own niggling problems that they'll pester you with.

Overall, I've enjoyed it, but that's not too surprising considering that I also enjoyed the first two games.

List of cons I've found so far:
- Usual Spiderweb problem of minimal sound and perhaps too few sprites for the game.
- Suffers from lack of proof-reading (at least 7 or 8 spelling mistakes that I've found so far, along with a bit of strange grammar at times)
